byTheNumbers.title: The year in numbers
byTheNumbers.standfirst: The census of 1921, taken the spring after this year, counted 318 million people, about nine in ten of them in villages.

items.title: Population
items.summary: The 1921 census counted more than 318 million people at a density of 177 per square mile.

sources.label: People's Archive of Rural India: Census of India 1921, Volume I, Part I, Report (summary)

items.title: Town and village
items.summary: About 10.2 percent of people lived in towns and 89.8 percent in villages.

sources.label: People's Archive of Rural India: Census of India 1921, Volume I, Part I, Report (summary)

items.metric: Share of people living in urban places

byTheNumbers.scarcityNote: Literacy, life expectancy and household electricity could not be traced to a source we opened for 1920-21. The two figures below are for the 1921 census.

foodAndKitchen.title: Food and the kitchen
foodAndKitchen.standfirst: The staples' prices are on the Prices board.

items.title: Rice, wheat or millet
items.summary: What filled the plate depended on the region: rice in the east and south, wheat and millet in much of the north and west.

items.title: The clay stove
items.summary: Most kitchens cooked on a clay chulha fed with wood, dung cakes or charcoal, and smoke was part of the day.

items.title: Eating with the right hand
items.summary: Meals were commonly served on a metal plate or a banana leaf and eaten by hand, with water in a brass vessel beside it.

clothingAndStyle.title: What people wore
clothingAndStyle.standfirst: The cloth people wore was itself the year's political question; see the spotlight.

items.title: Dhoti, kurta and turban
items.summary: Men in towns and villages wore the dhoti or lungi with a kurta or angarkha, and a turban or cap whose style told region and community.

items.title: The sari with a blouse
items.summary: Women wore the sari, draped in regional ways; the blouse and petticoat worn under it had spread through well-off households since the late 1800s.

items.title: Chappals, jootis and bare feet
items.summary: Leather chappals and jootis were common among those who could afford them, and many villagers went barefoot.

workAndWages.title: Work and wages
workAndWages.standfirst: Bombay's mill hands worked a ten-hour day after the strikes of early 1920, and workers began to organise.

items.title: A mill hand, Bombay Presidency (men)
items.summary: Men in the cotton mills earned on average about Rs 33 a month in 1921, the first year the Labour Office measured it.

sources.label: Clemens Dutt, Labour in India (1923), Marxists Internet Archive
Report on an enquiry into wages and hours of labour in the cotton mill industry, 1926 (Labour Office, Bombay), via EconBiz

items.job: Cotton-mill worker, men, Bombay Presidency average
items.originalUnits: Rs 33 a month (about 44 shillings at the time); 16 annas = 1 rupee

items.title: A mill hand, Bombay Presidency (women)
items.summary: Women in the cotton mills earned on average about Rs 16 a month in 1921, half the men's figure.

sources.label: Clemens Dutt, Labour in India (1923), Marxists Internet Archive
Report on an enquiry into wages and hours of labour in the cotton mill industry, 1926 (Labour Office, Bombay), via EconBiz

items.job: Cotton-mill worker, women, Bombay Presidency average

items.title: Twelve hours down to ten
items.summary: After the strike of 1920 mill basic wages rose in April 1920 and hours were cut from 12 to 10; the source describes the Sholapur mills.

sources.label: Report on an enquiry into wages and hours of labour in the cotton mill industry, 1926 (Labour Office, Bombay), via EconBiz

items.title: Tram workers organise
items.summary: Calcutta's tramway employees formed their first association in 1920.

workAndWages.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced wage rates outside the Bombay mills, nor figures for women's or child labour.

schoolAndChildhood.title: Growing up
schoolAndChildhood.standfirst: National schools were opened during the year; see the history section.

items.title: Education passes to the provinces
items.summary: Under the Government of India Act 1919, education became a provincial subject handled by Indian ministers.

items.title: Universities of the non-cooperation years
items.summary: Jamia Millia Islamia and Gujarat Vidyapith were founded in 1920 as national institutions outside the government system.

items.title: Few could read
items.summary: Literacy was below ten percent of the population, and far lower for girls.

gettingAround.title: Getting around
gettingAround.standfirst: Bombay's double-decker electric trams entered service in September 1920 at a fare of about one and a half annas.

items.title: Double-decker trams
items.summary: Bombay's electric trams, running since 1907, were joined by double-decker cars in September 1920.

sources.label: Live History India: Bombay's Tryst with Trams

items.title: The Bombay tram fare
items.summary: The fare rose from 1 anna in 1901 to 1½ annas in 1921, and to 2 annas by 1935.

sources.label: Live History India: Bombay's Tryst with Trams

gettingAround.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1920 railway fares or journey times.

keepingInTouch.title: Keeping in touch
keepingInTouch.standfirst: The weekly press carried the news of the movement.

items.title: The letter writer outside the post office
items.summary: Many people could not write, so scribes sat outside post offices and wrote postcards and letters for a few coins.

items.title: The telegram means bad news
items.summary: Telegrams were for emergencies and were costly, so a telegram at the door often meant a death or an illness.

items.title: Newspapers as political voice
items.summary: Gandhi began editing the weekly Young India in 1919, and papers like it carried the non-cooperation campaign to towns and readers' groups.

healthAndMedicine.title: Health and medicine
healthAndMedicine.standfirst: India was still counting the cost of the influenza of 1918, and cholera and plague had not gone away.

items.title: The influenza of 1918
items.summary: The influenza pandemic killed at least 12 million people in India, about 5 percent of the population, almost all of them between September and December 1918; estimates run as high as 17-18 million.

sources.label: Gateway House: The 1918 flu in India

sensitivity.note: This item describes epidemic disease and loss of life.

items.title: Influenza in the Bombay Presidency
items.summary: A Bombay review estimated 1,041,481 influenza deaths in the Presidency in 1918; by 1923 fewer than 1,000 deaths were returned to the disease.

sources.label: Bombay 1923-24: A review of the administration of the Presidency (Qatar Digital Library)

sensitivity.note: This item describes epidemic disease and loss of life.

items.title: Cholera
items.summary: Cholera epidemics were severe in Bombay in 1900, 1906, 1912 and 1919, and in several provinces outbreaks accompanied or followed the influenza.

sources.label: Bombay 1923-24: A review of the administration of the Presidency (Qatar Digital Library)

sensitivity.note: This item describes epidemic disease and loss of life.

healthAndMedicine.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced doctor fees, hospital provision or vaccination figures for 1920.

leisureAndFun.title: Evenings, weekends and festivals
leisureAndFun.standfirst: Indian cinema was silent; Raja Harishchandra (1913) had started it and films were shown with live music in theatres in the big cities.

items.title: Silent films
items.summary: Indian cinema was silent; Raja Harishchandra (1913) had started it and films were shown with live music in theatres in the big cities.

items.title: Parsi theatre
items.summary: Travelling Parsi theatre companies staged musical dramas in Urdu, Gujarati and Hindi in Bombay and beyond.

items.title: The gramophone
items.summary: Gramophone records of classical singers and stage songs were sold in towns from the early 1900s, and the gramophone was a prized possession.

items.title: Football in Calcutta
items.summary: Mohun Bagan won the IFA Shield in 1911, and football matches drew big crowds in Calcutta's maidans.

spotlight.title: Swadeshi at home: khadi and the boycott of foreign cloth
spotlight.standfirst: From 1919 Gandhi spun in public, and in 1920 the call to wear hand-spun, hand-woven khadi became the daily face of the non-cooperation movement.

items.title: Gandhi takes up the spinning wheel
items.summary: Gandhi began spinning at Mani Bhavan in Bombay in 1919 and encouraged others to do so; Wikipedia dates the khadi movement itself to 1918.

items.title: Khadi instead of foreign cloth
items.summary: A central idea of non-cooperation was to replace foreign cloth with hand-spun, hand-woven khadi.

items.title: A part for women
items.summary: When the movement began in 1920 Gandhi first gave women a limited part, boycott and swadeshi, but women claimed a larger role.

sources.label: RAU's IAS: Women in the freedom struggle

items.title: A fatwa on boycott
items.summary: On 8 September 1920 the Jamiat Ulama-i-Hind issued the Fatwa Tark-e-Mawalat urging a boycott of British goods, signed by 500 scholars.

items.title: The first bonfire
items.summary: On 31 July 1921, a year on, Gandhi lit a pile of foreign cloth at the Elphinstone Mill in Bombay before ten to twelve thousand people.

sources.label: The Wire: When a peaceful non-cooperation meeting in Bombay turned violent

spotlight.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced figures for khadi output or prices in 1920, so the section describes the campaign, not its economics.
